note: Our own explainer for a skill, shown the moment she gets one wrong. First-party and bundled, so it costs nothing, needs no account and works offline — the AoPS chapter is the paid-or-free extra beside it, not the only way back in. Written to a ten-year-old: short sentences, one method, and the trap named out loud. `links` are site-scoped searches rather than deep links, because a deep link that 404s two years from now is worse than a search that always lands.
links_note: free: true means no account and no payment. Anything marked false costs money to use properly.

Main idea.what: What the whole passage is about — not one interesting thing in it.
how: Say the passage back in one sentence, in your head, before looking at the choices.
A right answer covers the beginning, middle AND end. A wrong one covers only a bit.
Cross out any choice that is true but small.
Main idea.trap: The most tempting wrong answer is usually a real detail from the passage. True is not the same as main.

links.name: BBC Bitesize
links.q: main idea of a text KS2

Supporting detail/evidence.what: Something the passage actually says — findable, word for word.
how: Find the line. Do not answer from memory.
Put your finger on the sentence that proves it before you pick.
If you cannot find a line for it, it is not the answer.
Supporting detail/evidence.trap: A choice that sounds sensible and is true about the world, but is never said in the passage.

Inference.what: Something the passage makes almost certain without saying it outright.
how: Ask: what must be true, given what it does say?
Stay close. An inference is one small step, not a big guess.
You should still be able to point at the lines that force it.
Inference.trap: Going too far. If you need to invent anything at all, it is a guess, not an inference.

Organization/logic.what: How the parts of the passage fit together — why this paragraph comes after that one.
how: Give each paragraph a job in three words: sets it up, gives an example, argues back, sums up.
Then ask what the question is asking about: one paragraph, or how two relate?
Words like but, however, for example and so are the joins. Circle them.
Organization/logic.trap: Answering about what a paragraph SAYS when the question asked what it DOES.

Vocabulary in context.what: What a word means in THIS sentence — which may not be its usual meaning.
how: Cover the word. Read the sentence and say your own word in the gap.
Now find the choice closest to your word.
Put each choice back into the sentence and read it aloud.
Vocabulary in context.trap: Picking the word's most common meaning. The question exists because the passage is using a less common one.

Tone/style/figurative language.what: How the writer feels about it, and the tricks they use to show you.
how: Look at the adjectives and the verbs — that is where feeling hides.
Decide first whether it is warm, cold, or neutral. Then pick the closest word.
A comparison with like or as is a simile; without them it is a metaphor.
Tone/style/figurative language.trap: Choosing a very strong word — furious, terrified — when the passage is only mildly anything. Most writing is mild.

Perimeter.what: The distance all the way round the outside of a shape.
how: Walk the edge in your head and add every side you step along.
A rectangle has four: length + width + length + width, which is 2 x (length + width).
Going backwards? Take off the two sides you know, then halve what is left.
Perimeter.trap: Multiplying. Length x width is the area — the space inside — not the walk around the edge.

example.q: A banner is 10 cm by 3 cm. What is its perimeter?
example.work: 10 + 3 + 10 + 3 = 26 cm. (10 x 3 = 30 would be the area.)

Area.what: How much flat space is inside a shape.
how: Rectangle: length x width — think of the squares that would fill it.
Triangle: half of base x height, because a triangle is half a rectangle.
Given the area and one side, divide to get the other side back.
Area.trap: Forgetting the half on a triangle, and adding sides instead of multiplying.

example.q: A triangular flag has base 10 cm and height 6 cm.
example.work: Half of 10 x 6 = half of 60 = 30 cm2. (60 is the whole rectangle.)

Angles.what: How far something turns, measured in degrees.
how: The three angles of any triangle add to 180.
Angles on a straight line add to 180; all the way round a point is 360.
Given two angles of a triangle, subtract both from 180.
Angles.trap: Using 360 for a triangle. A triangle is 180 — a four-sided shape is 360.

example.q: A triangle has angles 45 and 60. What is the third?

Percent.what: A number out of a hundred. 25% means 25 for every 100.
how: Percent of a number: turn the percent into a fraction over 100, then multiply.
Learn the easy ones by heart: 50% is half, 25% is a quarter, 10% is divide by ten.
Build harder ones from those: 30% is three lots of 10%.
Percent.trap: Finding the percent when the question asked what the whole was, or the other way round. Say out loud which number is the whole.

Fractions.what: Part of a whole. The bottom says how many pieces; the top says how many you have.
how: Adding or subtracting: make the bottoms match first, then only the tops change.
Multiplying: tops together, bottoms together. No matching needed.
Dividing by a fraction: flip it over and multiply.
Fractions.trap: Adding the bottoms. A half plus a quarter is not two sixths.

Decimals.what: Another way of writing fractions, using place value after a dot.
how: Line up the dots before adding or subtracting — always.
Multiplying: ignore the dots, multiply, then count how many digits came after dots altogether.
0.5 is a half, 0.25 a quarter, 0.1 a tenth.
Decimals.trap: Thinking 0.35 is bigger than 0.5 because it has more digits. Compare place by place.

Whole-number operations.what: Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing ordinary numbers, carefully.
how: Line up the columns by place value before you start.
Estimate first: 2,400 + 1,750 is about 4,000, so an answer near 400 or 40,000 is wrong.
Check the answer against your estimate before moving on.
Whole-number operations.trap: A single place-value slip. Estimating first catches almost all of them.

Order of operations.what: Which part of a long sum to do first.
how: Brackets first, then multiply and divide, then add and subtract.
Multiply and divide are equal — do them left to right.
So are add and subtract. Left to right again.
Order of operations.trap: Working strictly left to right through everything, which gets 2 + 3 x 4 wrong.

Parity.what: Whether a number is odd or even, and what happens when you combine them.
how: Even + even = even. Odd + odd = even. Odd + even = odd.
Anything multiplied by an even number is even.
Odd x odd is the only way to keep a product odd.
Parity.trap: Assuming odd + odd is odd. Two odds always make an even.

Number sense.what: Knowing roughly what the answer should be before you work it out.
how: Round each number to something easy and do the easy sum first.
Ask whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than what you started with.
Then compare your real answer to that. If they disagree, one of them is wrong.
Number sense.trap: Trusting a worked answer that is wildly the wrong size. The estimate is the check.

Geometry.what: Shapes, their sides and angles, and what stays true about them.
how: Draw it, even roughly. Most geometry mistakes are picture mistakes.
Label every length and angle you are given, on the drawing.
Then ask which rule connects what you have to what you want.
Geometry.trap: Answering from the picture looking about right instead of from the numbers given.

Algebraic reasoning.what: Working with a number you do not know yet, usually called a letter.
how: Write the sentence as a sum, with a letter where the unknown goes.
Do the same thing to both sides until the letter is alone.
Put your answer back into the original sentence and check it works.
Algebraic reasoning.trap: Changing one side and not the other. Whatever you do, do it to both.

Mean.what: The average: share everything out equally.
how: Add every number together.
Divide by how many numbers there were.
Check: the mean must land between the smallest and the largest.
Mean.trap: Dividing by the wrong count. Count the numbers, not the total.

links.name: Khan Academy
links.q: mean average of a data set

Median.what: The middle number once they are in order.
how: Put them in order first. Always.
Odd count: the one in the middle. Even count: the mean of the middle two.
Cross off from both ends together until you meet.
Median.trap: Taking the middle of the list as written, without sorting it.

example.work: Already in order, five numbers, so the third: 59.

Mode.what: The value that appears most often.
how: Count how many times each value appears.
The one with the highest count is the mode.
There can be two modes, or none at all.
Mode.trap: Giving how many times it appeared instead of the value itself.

Range.what: How spread out the numbers are: largest minus smallest.
how: Find the biggest and the smallest.
Subtract.
The range is one number, not a pair.
Range.trap: Writing it as "5 to 20". The range of that is 15.

how: Add them all, divide by how many.
If the average and the count are given, multiply to get the total back.
Check the answer sits between the smallest and largest.
Average.trap: Forgetting that a missing value can be found by working backwards from the total.

Volume.what: How much space is inside a solid.
how: A box: length × width × height.
Think of it as the area of the bottom, stacked up as many layers as it is tall.
Units are cubed.
Volume.trap: Adding the three numbers, or multiplying only two of them.

Volume reasoning.what: Working backwards from a volume, or comparing two solids.
how: Volume = length × width × height, so divide by the two you know to find the third.
Doubling one side doubles the volume; doubling all three makes it eight times.
Same volume does not mean same shape.
Volume reasoning.trap: Assuming two boxes with the same volume must have the same surface area.

Probability.what: How likely something is, written as a fraction.
how: Top: how many ways it can happen. Bottom: how many ways anything can happen.
Count the total carefully — it is every item, not just the ones you want.
Always between 0 and 1.
Probability.trap: Putting the wrong number on the bottom. 4 red and 6 blue means 10 on the bottom, not 6.

how: Divide the total by how many there were.
Say the units out loud: dollars per item, miles per hour.
To compare two deals, get both down to one.
Unit rate.trap: Dividing the wrong way round. The thing you want "per" goes on the bottom.

Ratio.what: How two amounts compare, part to part.
how: 3 : 2 means for every 3 of the first there are 2 of the second.
Total parts = 3 + 2 = 5. Divide the whole by 5 to find one part.
Scale both sides by the same number to keep the ratio.
Ratio.trap: Treating 3 : 2 as 3 out of 2. It is 3 out of 5.

Scale.what: A drawing or model where every length is multiplied by the same number.
how: Find the scale factor: real length ÷ drawing length.
Multiply to go from drawing to real; divide to come back.
Every length uses the same factor.
Scale.trap: Applying the factor to some measurements but not others.

Scale reasoning.what: What happens to area and volume when you scale a shape.
how: Double every length and the area goes up four times.
Double every length and the volume goes up eight times.
Lengths × k, areas × k², volumes × k³.
Scale reasoning.trap: Assuming doubling the sides doubles the area. It quadruples it.

Measurement.what: Converting between units without losing track.
how: Write the conversion you know: 1 foot = 12 inches.
Going to smaller units, multiply. Going to bigger units, divide.
Check the size: inches should be a bigger number than feet.
Measurement.trap: Multiplying when you should divide. Ask first whether the answer should get bigger or smaller.

Coordinates.what: Finding a point on a grid using two numbers.
how: (x, y): along the corridor first, then up the stairs.
Distance along a flat line is just the difference of the numbers.
Plot the points before answering — always draw it.
Coordinates.trap: Swapping x and y. The first number is sideways.

Algebra.what: Using a letter for a number you do not know yet.
how: Turn the sentence into a sum with a letter in it.
Do the same thing to both sides until the letter stands alone.
Substitute your answer back in and check.
Algebra.trap: Doing something to one side and forgetting the other.

Expression.what: A sum with a letter in it, which you evaluate rather than solve.
how: Replace the letter with the number given.
Then follow the order of operations: brackets, multiply/divide, add/subtract.
There is no equals sign to balance — just work it out.
Expression.trap: Trying to solve for the letter when the question only asked you to put a number in.

Exponents.what: A small raised number saying how many times to multiply.
how: 4³ means 4 × 4 × 4, not 4 × 3.
Anything to the power 1 is itself; to the power 0 is 1.
Work out the power before multiplying or adding.
Exponents.trap: Multiplying the base by the exponent. 4³ is 64, not 12.

how: Learn 1 to 15 by heart — they come up constantly.
A square number is the area of a square with whole sides.

Square roots.what: The number that was multiplied by itself to get this one.
how: √49 asks: what times itself makes 49? 7.
If it is not a perfect square, find the two whole numbers it sits between.
Squaring and square-rooting undo each other.
Square roots.trap: Halving instead of rooting. √36 is 6, not 18.

Factors.what: Numbers that divide into it exactly, with nothing left over.
how: Go up in pairs from 1: 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4.
Stop when the pair meets in the middle.
Every number has 1 and itself as factors.
Factors.trap: Mixing up factors with multiples. Factors are smaller; multiples are bigger.

Multiples.what: What you get counting up in steps of that number.
how: Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, and on forever.
A common multiple appears in both lists.
The lowest common multiple is the first one they share.
Multiples.trap: Calling a factor a multiple. Multiples are the bigger ones.

Divisibility.what: Quick tests for whether one number divides another.
how: 2: ends even. 5: ends 0 or 5. 10: ends 0.
3: the digits add to a multiple of 3. 9: they add to a multiple of 9.
4: the last two digits make a multiple of 4.
Divisibility.trap: Doing the whole division when a digit test would have answered it in two seconds.

Prime factors.what: Breaking a number into the primes that multiply to make it.
how: Split it into any two factors, then keep splitting.
Stop when every branch is prime.
Every number has exactly one prime factorisation.
Prime factors.trap: Stopping too early and leaving a number that can still be split.

Remainders.what: What is left over when a division does not come out exactly.
how: Divide as far as whole numbers go, then see what is left.
The remainder is always smaller than what you divided by.
Check: divisor × answer + remainder = the number you started with.
Remainders.trap: Giving a remainder bigger than the divisor — that means the answer was too small.

Division.what: Sharing into equal groups, or asking how many fit.
how: Ask which it is: how many each, or how many groups?
Estimate first so you know roughly what to expect.
Multiply back to check.
Division.trap: Dividing the wrong way round. The whole goes inside the bracket.

Number properties.what: Facts that stay true about numbers whatever the numbers are.
how: Try it with small numbers first — 2, 3, 10.
If you can find one case where it fails, it is false.
Odd and even, positive and negative, zero and one behave in fixed ways.
Number properties.trap: Testing only one example and assuming it always holds.

how: Call the first one n; the next are n+1, n+2.
Their total is the middle one times how many there are, when the count is odd.
Consecutive even or odd numbers go up in twos.
Consecutive integers.trap: Writing n, n+1, n+2 for consecutive EVEN numbers. Those go n, n+2, n+4.

Pattern.what: A sequence built by the same rule each step.
how: Find the difference between one term and the next.
Same difference each time? Keep adding it. Doubling? It is multiplying.
Write the rule in words before using it.
Pattern.trap: Guessing from the first two terms. Check the rule against a third.

Estimation.what: A rough answer, quickly, to check the real one.
how: Round each number to something easy.
Do the easy sum in your head.
Compare it with your worked answer — they should be close.
Estimation.trap: Rounding both numbers the same way and forgetting the estimate is now always high or always low.

Data.what: Reading a table, chart or graph without misreading it.
how: Read the title and both axis labels before anything else.
Check what one square or one step on the scale is worth.
Find the number the question asks for; do not eyeball it.
Data.trap: Assuming each gridline is 1 when the scale says 5.

Data reasoning.what: Drawing a conclusion from a chart or a set of numbers.
how: Say what the data shows in one plain sentence first.
Only then look at the choices.
A conclusion must follow from the numbers, not from what seems likely.
Data reasoning.trap: Choosing an answer that is probably true in real life but is not shown by this data.

Symmetry.what: A shape that folds onto itself exactly.
how: Imagine folding along a line — do the halves match?
A square has four lines of symmetry; a rectangle has two.
Rotational symmetry is turning, not folding.
Symmetry.trap: Counting a diagonal as a line of symmetry on a rectangle. It is not.

Mixed reasoning.what: A question that needs more than one idea joined together.
how: Work out what you are actually being asked for, in words.
List what you were given, and what each piece lets you find.
Do it one step at a time, writing each result down.
Mixed reasoning.trap: Trying to leap straight to the answer. Two small steps beat one guess.
